title: Trainable Quantum-Native Language Models: Dissipative Memory, Capacity Limits, and Hardware Validation
abstract: We study byte-level autoregressive language models whose hidden state is a small quantum register, whose transitions are learned token-conditioned quantum channels, and whose next-byte probabilities come directly from Born-rule measurements without a learned classical vocabulary projection or softmax. In the fixed-width recurrent setting, unitary dynamics cannot contract or reset stored distinctions; experimentally, unitary recurrence loses to its retrained one-token control in every tested variant. Introducing learned dissipation, then token-conditioned dissipative gating, yields useful memory beyond one token. The gated model improves test negative log-likelihood by 0.20 +/- 0.03 nats/byte over retrained parameter-matched one-token controls at context length 12, and by 0.29-0.33 at longer contexts, but never beats retrained two-token controls. A key-value recall benchmark shows a width-dependent threshold: one stored pair meets the pre-registered accuracy bar at 4-5 memory qubits, two pairs at 6-7, and three pairs remain unsolved. This is consistent with, but does not establish, a capacity explanation for the short effective memory horizon. As a secondary result, one-qubit models reach lower stationary memory entropy than a heuristically optimized classical predictive frontier at matched error in 9/9 seeds. On IBM Heron hardware, computational-basis memory-register distributions show signal against a uniform null in 12/12 circuits across prefixes of up to 12 tokens, next-bit probabilities pass pre-registered accuracy bars at four-token prefixes, and bytes are generated autoregressively by sampling physically measured bit probabilities. The tested models are classically simulable and substantially worse than classical n-gram baselines. We claim no computational quantum advantage.
summary: This paper proposes and tests quantum-native language models where the memory state is a small quantum register whose evolution is controlled by learned quantum channels. By incorporating dissipation, the model achieves useful, context-dependent memory, demonstrating performance gains over purely unitary approaches. The work validates this architecture end-to-end on quantum hardware while concluding that no computational quantum advantage is demonstrated over classical baselines.
main_problem: The paper investigates the necessary memory dynamics for trainable quantum-native recurrent language models, assessing their capacity limits and validating the architecture on current quantum hardware.
main_result: Introducing learned, token-conditioned dissipation significantly improves memory retention over purely unitary dynamics, allowing the model to solve key-value recall tasks up to two stored pairs using a small quantum register.
method: The authors train the model by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the next byte, using quantum channels (CPTP maps) to govern the state evolution and direct Born-rule measurements for output probabilities.
model_or_system: The model uses a small quantum register ($ho_t$) as its hidden state, with transitions governed by learned, token-conditioned quantum channels. The output probability is read directly from the measurement expectation value, bypassing classical vocabulary projections.
key_observables: Negative log-likelihood (NLL) improvement (e.g., +0.20 nats/byte), key-value recall accuracy (e.g., 2 pairs at 6-7 qubits), and physical measurement of bit probabilities on hardware.
important_parameters: Context length (up to 12 tokens), quantum register width (4-7 qubits), and the comparison between unitary vs. dissipative channels.
main_assumptions: The tested models are classically simulable at the tested widths, and the primary limitation is an empirical two-token memory horizon, not a proven fundamental capacity law.
figures_summary: The notes detail comparisons between different memory dynamics (unitary vs. dissipative) and show quantitative performance gains across various context lengths and memory tasks.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the failure of unitary recurrence, then introducing and testing learned dissipation/gating mechanisms, benchmarking memory capacity via key-value recall, and finally validating the full pipeline on real quantum hardware.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses how non-unitary, dissipative dynamics—which are central to open quantum systems theory—can be engineered into a functional, trainable computational primitive for complex tasks like language modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The three memory dynamics compared. UMW: unitary conjugation (norm-preserving, cannot contract stored distinctions). UMW-D: unitary write followed by a fixed learned dis- sipation channel (a work qubit coupled, reset, and discarded). UMW-G: one learned CPTP map per token, writing and forgetting jointly. All rows read out with the same 256-outcome Born-rule POVM, with no softmax; the sampled byte is the next input.

Figure 2: Full recurrence against retrained one-token (h1) and two-token (h2) controls of the same parameterization and parameter count; dots are individual seeds, bars their means. Dotted and dashed lines: the tuned bigram (2.3406) and the classical 4-gram (1.5125) on the same test set.

Figure 3: Key–value recall ladder (exp 295, single seed). Left: answer accuracy against width for K = 1, 2, 3 stored pairs, with the 0.5 bar and the value-marginal floor. Right: value content and full configuration entropy of the largest K solved at each width, with the single-copy accessible-information ceiling of n bits drawn as an information-scale reference only, not as a task-solvability threshold.

Figure 4: Perturbed coin, one memory qubit: stationary memory entropy S(¯ρ) against excess prediction error, for trained models without (dark) and with (teal) the annealed entropy penalty; markers denote p = 0.3 (circle), 0.4 (square), 0.45 (triangle). Grey curves: the attacked classical frontier per p; dashed: Cµ = ln 2; dotted: the quantum optima Cq(p).
